title: Nuclear scattering phase shifts with factorized geometric-time RODEO on a quantum processor
authors: Myeong-Hwan Mun, Jubin Park, Myung-Ki Cheoun, Eunja Ha
abstract: We reconstruct elastic $s$-wave neutron-proton ($np$) phase shifts from trapped spectra measured on IBM Aachen using a compressed RODEO circuit. For a schematic square-well interaction represented by classically constructed four-dimensional effective Hamiltonians, four positive-energy levels at five trap strengths supply twenty inputs to classical modified effective range expansion (MERE) extrapolation to free space. The six-cycle factorized geometric-time RODEO implementation (FG-R6) combines ancilla reuse, exact query-phase separation, post-compilation binding, and six numerically optimized geometric evolution times. Numerical cycle-count tests support this choice within the adopted local spectral tolerances. At the same three-qubit width and equal shot budgets, FG-R6 reduces median compiled depth and two-qubit-gate count by 33.1% and 37.2% relative to ten-cycle dynamic direct RODEO (direct R10), increases the median fitted amplitude, and lowers median finite-shot energy uncertainty from 0.610 to 0.534 keV. For this dataset's primary fit on the 0.1-30.0 MeV grid, the maximum central phase-shift deviation from exact-energy MERE decreases from $0.842^\circ$ to $0.163^\circ$, despite a larger root-mean-square (RMS) trapped-energy deviation. The full-grid gain arises mainly in the low-energy extrapolation region; direct R10 has slightly smaller residuals relative to the same reference on the 10.0-30.0 MeV common energy-interpolation subset. The FG-R6 central curve differs from the analytical square-well solution by at most $0.156^\circ$. Fit-form sensitivity remains appreciable and is assessed separately from finite-shot uncertainty. This reduced-space benchmark connects RODEO circuit compression to nuclear continuum observables and shows why circuit performance must be assessed through the scattering reconstruction and its energy range, not spectral RMS errors alone.
summary: This research demonstrates a method to reconstruct neutron-proton scattering phase shifts by measuring trapped energy levels on a quantum processor. The authors introduce and validate a novel, resource-efficient quantum circuit implementation (FG-R6) that significantly reduces circuit depth and gate count compared to prior methods. This work establishes a rigorous benchmark showing that quantum algorithm performance must be evaluated based on the fidelity of the final physical observable, not just local energy measurements.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of reconstructing fundamental nuclear scattering phase shifts from trapped spectra using quantum processors.
main_result: A factorized geometric-time RODEO circuit (FG-R6) significantly outperforms a standard ten-cycle direct RODEO circuit (direct R10) in terms of quantum circuit resources and accuracy for phase shift reconstruction.
method: The authors compare two quantum circuit implementations (FG-R6 vs. direct R10) for the RODEO algorithm, utilizing circuit compression and geometric time evolution to measure energy levels and extrapolate scattering parameters.
model_or_system: The physical system is the elastic s-wave neutron-proton (np) interaction, modeled using a schematic square-well potential. Measurements are performed on trapped spectra using a quantum processor (IBM Aachen).
key_observables: Elastic s-wave neutron-proton phase shifts ($\delta_0$), median compiled depth, two-qubit-gate count, and maximum central phase-shift deviation.
important_parameters: Energy grid ranging from 0.1 to 30.0 MeV; circuit cycle counts (6 vs. 10); and various spectral tolerances.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on extrapolating trap-dependent energy levels to free space using the classical Modified Effective Range Expansion (MERE).
figures_summary: Figures compare the cycle structure of the two quantum circuits and show the reduction in phase-shift deviation achieved by FG-R6 compared to direct R10 across the energy grid.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem of phase shift reconstruction, details the two competing quantum circuit methods (R10 vs. FG-R6), presents quantitative comparisons of circuit resources and achieved accuracy, and concludes by emphasizing the importance of assessing circuit performance via the full scattering reconstruction.
why_interesting: This work directly connects the abstract performance metrics of quantum algorithms (circuit depth, gate count) to a concrete, physically measurable observable (nuclear scattering phase shifts), providing a crucial benchmark for quantum simulation in nuclear physics.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

figures.caption: Figure 1: Representative cycles of the ancilla-recycled RODEO circuits. (a) Dynamic direct R10 uses ten cycles and compiles the query-dependent controlled evolution separately for each query energy. (b) FG–R6 uses six geometric evolution times and a reference-energy circuit with the query-dependent ancilla phase bound after compilation. Both use two system qubits and one recycled ancilla. M/R denotes measurement after each cycle and reset before the next; no reset follows the final cycle. System qubits are measured only at the end, and classical ancilla records are omitted for clarity. The displayed cycle is included in the total of R cycles; trial-state preparation is performed only once....

Figure 2: Compiled resources on ibm_aachen for dynamic direct R10 and FG– R6. Circuit depth, two-qubit-gate count, and total operation count are shown as medians over 160 circuits per implementation after compilation to the backend instruction set architecture (ISA). Both implementations use three active qubits.

Figure 3: Free-space phase shifts reconstructed from raw IBM measurements. (a) Direct R10 and FG–R6 results from twenty trapped levels per method, compared with the analytical square-well solution and exact-energy MERE. (b) Residuals relative to the exact-energy MERE reference, ∆δ0 = δQPU 0 −δref 0 . Shading denotes pointwise 16–84% finite-shot bootstrap intervals, excluding fit-form sensitivity, cross-target covariance, and run-to-run drift. Symbols identify reconstructed curves, not independent continuum measurements. The dotted line at E = 9.9566 MeV marks the onset of common energy interpolation; trap removal remains an extrapolation throughout. Maxima use E = 0.1, 0.2, . . . , 30.0 MeV.
